introduction-thinking-like-a-mechanic.core: Mechanical sympathy means writing software that works with the hardware rather than against it. CPUs are fast only when data is in cache and branches are predictable; memory is slow and organised in cache lines and NUMA nodes; cores share caches and contend for cache lines. Code that ignores this can be 10–100× slower than code doing the same work with hardware-friendly layouts and access patterns.

first_principles.problem: Two algorithms with the same Big-O complexity differ 20× in speed on real hardware.

analogy.title: A racing driver who understands the engine
analogy.story: Knowing how the car works lets the driver shift at the right moment instead of fighting the machine.
analogy.breaks: Cars are similar across models; CPUs differ in cache sizes and microarchitecture.

check.q: Why can two O(n²) loops over the same array differ 10× in speed?
check.a: Different access orders hit cache lines efficiently or not, so memory latency dominates the slower version.

the-great-lie-memory-is-fast.core: Programming models present memory as a flat, uniformly fast array. In reality a modern CPU can execute hundreds of instructions in the time one DRAM access takes (~100 ns, roughly 300+ cycles). Caches hide that latency only when access patterns are predictable and data fits. 'Memory-bound' code spends most cycles stalled waiting for data, not computing, so reducing memory traffic often matters more than reducing arithmetic.

first_principles.problem: A team optimises arithmetic in a hot loop, but profiling shows the CPU stalls on memory 70% of the time.

analogy.title: A chef whose pantry is down the street
analogy.story: Chopping speed doesn't matter if every ingredient requires a walk to the pantry.
analogy.breaks: Chefs can carry several items; CPUs fetch fixed 64-byte lines.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Confirms memory, not math, is the bottleneck.

code.text:
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,LLC-load-misses ./app
#  instructions per cycle: 0.45   ← memory-bound (good code often > 2)
#  LLC-load-misses: 1.2e9

check.q: What does a low instructions-per-cycle (IPC) value suggest?
check.a: The CPU is often stalled, typically waiting on memory, so the code is memory-bound.

the-latency-hierarchy-the-desk-analogy.core: Approximate latencies: register ~0.3 ns, L1 cache ~1 ns (32–48 KB per core), L2 ~4 ns (around 1–2 MB), L3 ~10–20 ns (tens of MB, shared), DRAM ~80–120 ns, NVMe SSD ~20–100 µs, network within a data centre ~0.5 ms, cross-continent ~80 ms. Each level is roughly 3–10× slower and bigger. Performance comes from keeping the working set in the fastest level that fits.

first_principles.problem: Engineers can't reason about why a lookup table that fits in L2 beats a 'smarter' algorithm hitting DRAM.
truths: Each level is bigger and slower.
Working set size decides the level.

analogy.title: A desk, drawer, filing cabinet, warehouse
analogy.story: Papers on your desk take a second, the drawer a few seconds, the cabinet across the room a minute, and the warehouse across town an hour.
analogy.breaks: Desks are manually organised; caches are managed automatically by hardware.

branches.label: Rule
children: Fit working set in fastest level

check.q: Roughly how much slower is a DRAM access than an L1 cache hit?

cache-lines-and-spatial-locality.core: Caches move data in fixed 64-byte cache lines. Touching one byte loads its whole line, so neighbouring data comes for free (spatial locality), and hardware prefetchers detect sequential or strided access and fetch ahead. Arrays of contiguous structs or primitive arrays (structure of arrays) exploit this; linked lists and pointer-chasing trees scatter accesses across lines and defeat prefetching.

first_principles.problem: Iterating a linked list of 10 million nodes is 20× slower than iterating an array of the same values.

analogy.title: Buying eggs by the carton
analogy.story: You can't buy one egg; you get a carton, so recipes using neighbouring eggs are cheap.
analogy.breaks: Cartons are always 12; lines are 64 bytes (128 on some CPUs).

check.q: Why are linked lists slow to traverse compared with arrays?
check.a: Nodes are scattered in memory, so each step likely misses cache and defeats hardware prefetching.

false-sharing-the-noisy-neighbor-problem.core: Cache coherence works per cache line. If two threads on different cores write to different variables that share the same 64-byte line, each write invalidates the other core's copy, and the line ping-pongs between cores, even though the threads never touch the same data. Per-thread counters packed in an array are the classic case. The fix is padding or aligning hot per-thread data to separate cache lines.

first_principles.problem: A multi-threaded counter gets slower as more threads are added, despite each thread using its own counter.

analogy.title: Two people sharing one notebook page
analogy.story: Each writes in their own corner, but they must keep passing the notebook back and forth.
analogy.breaks: People could tear the page; hardware can't split a line.

check.q: How can two threads that never share variables still slow each other down?
check.a: If their variables share a cache line, each write invalidates the other's cached copy (false sharing).

numa-non-uniform-memory-access.core: Multi-socket servers attach memory to each socket. A core reading its local node's memory is fast; reading a remote node's memory crosses the interconnect, roughly 1.5–2× the latency with less bandwidth. Linux allocates on first touch, on the node of the thread that first writes the page. Threads migrating across sockets, or initialisation by one thread, cause remote access. Pin threads and memory together, or interleave memory for shared data.

first_principles.problem: A database on a 2-socket server performs worse than on a 1-socket machine because half its memory accesses are remote.

analogy.title: Two kitchens in one restaurant
analogy.story: A chef using the other kitchen's fridge walks further each time.
analogy.breaks: Chefs see the walk; NUMA penalties hide in latency.

code.text:
numactl --hardware            # node distances: 10 local, 21 remote
numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./redis-server
numastat -p $(pgrep redis)    # 'other_node' should be near 0
# shared data: numactl --interleave=all ./app

check.q: What is Linux's default NUMA memory allocation policy?
check.a: First touch: a page is allocated on the node of the CPU that first writes to it.

branch-prediction-and-speculation.core: Modern CPUs pipeline 15–20 stages and execute out of order, so they guess which way branches go and speculatively execute ahead. A correct prediction is nearly free; a misprediction flushes the pipeline, costing around 15–20 cycles. Predictable branches (sorted data, loop conditions) are cheap and random ones are expensive. Branchless code (conditional moves, arithmetic tricks), sorting data or restructuring loops can remove mispredictions.

first_principles.problem: Processing a sorted array is 5× faster than the same unsorted array with an if inside the loop.
truths: Pipelines need instructions ahead of time.

analogy.title: A waiter who guesses your order
analogy.story: Regulars' orders are prepared early and arrive instantly; a wrong guess means throwing food away and starting again.
analogy.breaks: Waiters ask; CPUs must guess every few nanoseconds.

check.q: Why does sorting data sometimes speed up a loop with an if statement?
check.a: The branch becomes predictable (long runs of true then false), so the CPU rarely mispredicts.

spectre-and-meltdown-when-speculation-be.core: Speculative execution leaves traces in caches even when the speculated work is discarded. Meltdown let user code speculatively read kernel memory and leak it through cache-timing side channels; it was fixed by kernel page-table isolation (KPTI). Spectre tricks speculation into accessing out-of-bounds or victim data; it's mitigated by fences, retpolines, IBRS and bounds masking. Those mitigations cost performance, especially for syscall-heavy workloads.

first_principles.problem: After a kernel update, a syscall-heavy service loses 15% throughput and nobody knows why.

analogy.title: A clerk who glances at a confidential file before checking permission
analogy.story: They put it back, but you can tell which drawer they opened by how warm the handle is.
analogy.breaks: Warm handles cool quickly; cache timing is precise and repeatable.

code.text:
grep . /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/*
# meltdown: Mitigation: PTI
# spectre_v2: Mitigation: Enhanced / Automatic IBRS; IBPB: conditional; RSB filling
perf stat -e syscalls:sys_enter_* -a sleep 5   # syscall rate drives KPTI cost

check.q: Why did Meltdown mitigations (KPTI) slow syscall-heavy workloads?
check.a: KPTI separates kernel and user page tables, adding overhead (TLB flushes, CR3 switches) on every user-kernel transition.

putting-it-all-together-hardware-sympath.core: Apply hardware sympathy methodically. Profile first (perf for IPC, cache misses, branch misses), find the hot path, then fix data layout (contiguous, struct-of-arrays, compact types), access patterns (sequential, batched), sharing (pad per-thread data, avoid contended locks), placement (NUMA pinning), and branches (predictable or branchless). Re-measure every change, since intuition about hardware is often wrong.

first_principles.problem: A team rewrites code 'for performance' based on guesses and gains nothing.

analogy.title: A pit crew with telemetry
analogy.story: They change tyres, wings or fuel strategy based on lap data, not hunches.
analogy.breaks: Race conditions are visible on track; CPU effects need counters.

example.title: Optimisation loop
flow: perf: IPC 0.4, LLC misses high in order matching

check.q: What's the first step before applying hardware-sympathy optimisations?
check.a: Profile with hardware counters to find the actual hot path and its bottleneck (cache misses, branch misses, contention).
